questions.q: What does this lesson mean by saying a postmortem template's "blameless" header is not the same thing as a blameless culture?
options: The word "blameless" is legally required on all incident documentation regardless of actual practice
Organizations can copy the format and the language without the underlying substance changing, so people still self-censor and reviews still informally search for who's at fault
Blameless postmortems were never actually described in Google's SRE book
The template format itself causes outages if used incorrectly
questions.explain: Copying the heading and 'no blame' wording doesn't guarantee the substance follows — in a culture with the template but not the practice, people still avoid being named and reviews still informally hunt for fault.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the real test of a blameless culture — more revealing than how a major outage gets written up?
options: Whether an engineer who notices a near-miss that almost became an incident feels safe enough to report it voluntarily, with no outage forcing the disclosure
Whether the postmortem document is formatted according to a style guide
Whether the incident was resolved within the SLA's stated time limit
Whether the postmortem was published within 24 hours of the incident
questions.explain: A major outage gets written up regardless, because it's already visible. The harder, more revealing test is whether people voluntarily disclose near-misses nobody would otherwise have noticed.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say blameless culture is fundamentally a leadership responsibility rather than a documentation exercise?
options: Documentation templates are maintained by a separate department from leadership
Leadership approval is only needed to publish the final postmortem PDF

Leadership's response the first time a respected engineer honestly discloses a mistake is the clearest real signal — a punishing reaction updates every witnessing engineer's calculus regardless of what the template says
Leadership is responsible for writing the blameless postmortem template itself
questions.explain: Trust in a blameless process is built through consistent leadership behavior that rewards disclosure, and it can be destroyed in a single incident where a punishing response is witnessed — something no template wording can control.

questions.q: Which trend in near-miss reporting rate does the lesson say is the real evidence of a lived blameless culture?
options: Near-miss reports should stay flat regardless of any cultural changes
Near-miss reports should decrease over time, since the culture should prevent near-misses entirely
Near-miss reporting rate is unrelated to psychological safety
Near-miss reports should increase over time, because people learn through direct experience that reporting one doesn't cost them anything
questions.explain: A rising rate of voluntary near-miss reports is a leading indicator that people have learned disclosure is genuinely safe — the opposite of what a declining or stagnant rate would suggest.

questions.q: The lesson suggests checking postmortems for whether they name systemic and process failures in concrete detail versus staying vague. What is this a signal of?
options: Whether the postmortem author is a senior or junior engineer
Whether vague language is replacing the specific places where a particular person's name would otherwise have appeared, a sign the blameless practice isn't fully real yet
Whether the incident caused revenue loss
Whether the postmortem template includes a timeline section
questions.explain: Staying vague in exactly the spots where naming a specific individual's action would otherwise be natural is a tell that the review is still informally protecting or avoiding blame, even under a blameless header.
